opus-5.5.text:
I think code is special because it's probably the most structured form of reasoning we have in natural data. When a model learns to write code, it isn't just learning syntax — it's learning how to break a big goal into smaller steps, keep track of state, call functions, read the result, and then adjust. That's basically what an agent does. An agent task is: you have an objective, you have tools, you take an action, the environment gives you feedback, and you decide the next step. Code has exactly that loop built in — write, execute, see the error, debug, try again.

So when people ask why code training transfers so well to agent tasks, my intuition is that the underlying "skeleton" is the same. Calling an API in a program and calling a tool as an agent are not that different from the model's perspective. Handling an exception in code and recovering from a failed action in a browser are, at some abstract level, the same skill.

Another point is verifiability. Code gives you a very clean signal — it runs or it doesn't, the test passes or it fails. That makes it one of the best domains for reinforcement learning, because the reward is relatively hard to hack. When you do RL on code, the model gets a lot of practice in long-horizon, multi-step problem solving with real feedback, and that kind of behavior — planning, self-checking, persisting through errors — seems to generalize beyond code itself.

But I'd also be careful not to overstate it. Code gives you strong generalization in the "logical execution" part of agents. What it doesn't fully give you is the messier part of the real world — ambiguous instructions, understanding what a user actually wants, dealing with environments that aren't deterministic. Those still need their own data and their own training. So I'd say code is like the foundation, or the backbone, of agent capability, but it's not the whole building. The next step is figuring out how to get that same kind of clean feedback loop in more open-ended domains.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to look at it is that code is, in a sense, the most honest form of reasoning data we have. When you write code, you can't be vague. Every step has to be explicit, every assumption has to be stated, and at the end there's a compiler or a test suite that tells you whether you were right. So a model that's been trained heavily on code has internalized a particular discipline: break a goal into sub-goals, keep track of state, handle edge cases, and verify the result. That's exactly the skeleton of what an agent has to do.

So when people ask why code training transfers to agent tasks that have nothing to do with programming, my answer is that the transfer isn't really about syntax or APIs. It's about the structure of long-horizon problem solving. A coding task is often the smallest natural example of a real agent loop: you read the environment, you form a plan, you act, you get feedback, you revise. Repeat that millions of times during training and the model learns something closer to a procedure than a fact.

There's a second piece, which is that code is where the model learns to use tools in the first place. Calling a function, reading what comes back, deciding what to do next, that pattern is identical whether the function is a sort routine or a browser or a database query. So the model doesn't need to learn tool use from scratch for each new agent setting; it already has the prior.

And the third thing I'd emphasize is verifiability. Code gives you dense, cheap, reliable reward signals, which is rare. You can do reinforcement learning at scale on it without a huge annotation effort. What we've seen is that the capabilities you sharpen there, like planning and self-correction and knowing when you're uncertain, show up afterward in domains where you never had that kind of clean signal. That's the real generalization, and honestly I think we're still early in understanding how far it goes.

astra-6.text:
I think the generalization comes less from learning the syntax of a programming language and more from learning how to turn an intention into a precise sequence of actions. To write code, a model has to break a problem down, track dependencies, and satisfy constraints. Those abilities are also useful when an agent needs to use tools or carry out a task over multiple steps.

Code also provides a useful feedback loop. You write something, execute it, see an error, and revise your approach. If training includes that process, it can teach a model to use feedback to make progress. For an agent, that matters because its first action may not succeed, and it needs to decide what to do next based on the result.

But I would distinguish being good at code from being good at acting in an environment. A model might generate an excellent plan and still struggle to execute it when the observations are incomplete or the tool behaves unexpectedly. So code training gives you a strong foundation for agent capabilities, but reliable generalization also requires training on interaction: taking actions, observing consequences, and recovering from mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think code training gives a model more than the ability to write code. It trains a way of solving problems: breaking a goal into steps, tracking how state changes, and understanding dependencies. Those abilities transfer quite naturally to agent tasks, where the model has to decide what to do, use a tool, observe the result, and then choose the next action.

Code also provides a useful feedback loop. A solution can look reasonable and still fail when you run it. Learning from that feedback can help a model revise its approach instead of simply producing a plausible answer. For an agent, that distinction is very important: success depends on what actually happens in the environment.

But I wouldn’t say that strong coding ability automatically produces a strong agent. Real environments have ambiguous goals, incomplete information, and actions whose effects may be difficult to reverse. So I see code training as a foundation for generalization, while interaction training is still needed to teach the model how to use those capabilities reliably.
